description: Hi, I'm the captain of the Team LUNE. We aim to develop solutions for monitoring and improving the health status of astronauts in space. If you believe in yourself, have good communication skills, basic required skills don't hasitate and join us!
summary:
crew-WELL is a software prototype for monitoring and recording astronauts' health on long-duration space missions. It brings vital-sign and environmental measurements into one dashboard with trend charts and a record history. Users can log data manually or by English voice check-in, which always shows the recognized result for approval, editing or cancellation before saving. A daily planner adds check-ins and user-defined reminders, a clearly labeled simulated sensor panel demonstrates future device integration, and a browser-based viewer explores NASA OSDR research data (OSD-575) separately from demo data.
Organized records and trends can help teams notice what needs attention and could supply useful data for scientific studies. crew-WELL offers reminders and points to watch, never diagnosis. It is an educational prototype, not a medical device, and uses simulated data with no live sensor connection.
These are only its first capabilities. We plan to integrate real sensor data from instruments placed inside a spacecraft or habitat, with proper validation, and to evolve crew-WELL into an intelligent, voice-driven crew-support assistant powered by a conversational AI model that can understand context, answer questions and proactively support astronauts' well-being.
details:
What it does and how it works
crew-WELL is a browser-based dashboard prototype for monitoring and recording astronaut health. It shows summary cards and trend charts for heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, sleep and environmental measurements, with a record history. Measurements can be entered manually or by an English voice check-in: the app repeats the recognized value and note, and nothing is saved until the user approves, edits or cancels. A daily planner supports movement, meal and fluid check-ins and user-defined reminders. A simulated sensor panel, clearly labeled as demo data, shows how future device integration could look. A separate viewer lets users load NASA OSDR research CSV files (OSD-575), choose a numeric field and chart it in the browser; the file is not uploaded.

Benefits
Records, trends and routines are in one place instead of scattered. Trends are easier to see than single values. User confirmation prevents misrecognized voice input from becoming a record. Research data is kept separate from demo data, so nothing is presented as live telemetry.

Intended impact
We want to help crews and support teams keep an organized health record, notice what needs attention through reminders and points to watch, and potentially supply useful data for scientific studies. crew-WELL never replaces a diagnosis. Next, we plan validated integration of real spacecraft sensors and a voice-driven AI crew-support assistant.

Tools and technologies
TypeScript and JavaScript, React, Vite, and CSS; Recharts for charts; the browser’s Web Speech API (SpeechRecognition / webkitSpeechRecognition) for optional voice check-ins; and localStorage for browser-local records and planner settings. npm is used to install dependencies and run builds. GitHub is used for version control, with GitHub Actions running build checks. The prototype runs in a web browser and requires no special hardware. Sensor values are simulated; no physical sensors are connected. GitHub Copilot assisted with coding. No separate design tool was used.

Creativity
Instead of only displaying numbers, crew-WELL combines health trends, daily routines, a confirmed voice check-in and open research data in one interface. The confirm-before-save voice flow and the clear separation of simulated and real research data are deliberate design choices for safety and honesty.

Factors our team considered
Safety and responsibility: it is not a medical device, gives reminders instead of diagnoses, and does not recommend medication or doses.

Privacy: browser records are not encrypted, so real or sensitive health data should not be entered. Transparency: simulated values are labeled everywhere.

Accessibility: manual entry works when voice recognition is unavailable.

Realism: real sensors would need compatible devices, secure data transfer, measurement quality and expert validation.
